'''''Chenopodium giganteum''''', also known as '''tree spinach''', is an annual, upright many-branched [[forb]] with a stem diameter of up to 5 cm at the base, that can grow to a height of up to 3 m.<ref name=":2">Zhu, Gelin & Mosyakin, Sergei & E. Clemants, Steven. (2003). Chenopodiaceae (Flora of China). in ''Flora of China'', Volume 5, Chapter: Chenopodiaceae, Beijing: Science Press & St. Louis: Missouri Botanical Garden Press, Wu Zhengyi, Peter H. Raven, pp. 351–414</ref>

==Description==
The younger leaves of ''Chenopodium giganteum'' are hairy with a magenta colour and the older become green. The [[Rhombus|rhombic]] to [[Ovate (leaf)|ovate]] formed [[Lamina (leaf)|lamina]] can have a surface of up to 20 x 16 cm. The [[inflorescence]] consists of terminal [[panicle]]s with [[hermaphrodite]] flowers, which are wind pollinated.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> The flowers contain 5 [[perianth]] leaves and 5 [[stamen]]s. The flowering period begins in August. The seeds have a diameter of 1.5 mm.<ref name=":2" /> The number of chromosomes is n=54.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Rana|first1=Tikam|last2=Narzary|first2=Diganta|last3=Ohri|first3=Deepak|date=2010-03-01|title=Genetic diversity and relationships among some wild and cultivated species of Chenopodium L. (Amaranthaceae) using RAPD and DAMD methods|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287508938|journal=Current Science|volume=98|pages=840–846}}</ref>

==Habitat and distribution==
''Chenopodium giganteum'' belongs to the same genus as [[quinoa]] or ''[[Chenopodium album]]''. Many species of this genus have a long history of domestications as grain, vegetable or forage crops.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bioversityinternational.org/e-library/publications/detail/chenopods-chenopodium-spp/|title=Chenopods, Chenopodium spp.|access-date=2018-11-14|language=en}}</ref> Therefore, genetic relationships and place of origin are hard to determine. ''Chenopodium giganteum'' has two main subspecies: one originating from India the other from America.<ref name=":3" />

It grows well in Mediterranean environment but needs full or partial shade. ''Chenopodium giganteum'' does not have high requirements on [[soil quality]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=De Santis|first1=Giuditta|last2=D’Ambrosio|first2=Tiziana|last3=Rinaldi|first3=Michele|last4=Rascio|first4=Agata|date=July 2016|title=Heritabilities of morphological and quality traits and interrelationships with yield in quinoa ( Chenopodium quinoa Willd.) genotypes in the Mediterranean environment|journal=Journal of Cereal Science|volume=70|pages=177–185|doi=10.1016/j.jcs.2016.06.003|issn=0733-5210}}</ref> Furthermore, it shows weedy characteristics such as fast growth and rapid spreading.<ref name=":4" /> In a few countries, such as Germany and Slovakia, ''Chenopodium giganteum'' has been reported as a [[neophyte (botany)|neophyte]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mendeley.com/catalogue/inventory-alien-flora-slovakia/|title=Inventory of the alien flora of Slovakia|last1=Medvecká|first1=Jana|last2=Kliment|first2=Ján|date=2012|website=www.mendeley.com|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-11-14|last3=Májeková|first3=Jana|last4=Halada|first4=Luboš|last5=Zaliberová|first5=Marica|last6=Gojdičová|first6=Ema|last7=Feráková|first7=Viera|last8=Jarolímek|first8=Ivan}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mendeley.com/catalogue/bemerkenswerte-neophytenfunde-aus-baden-w%C3%BCrttemberg-und-nachbargebieten-20042008/|title=Bemerkenswerte Neophytenfunde aus Baden- Württemberg und Nachbargebieten (2004–2008)|last=Amarell|first=Uwe|date=2010|website=www.mendeley.com|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-11-14}}</ref> The commercial cultivation of ''Chenopodium giganteum'' is nearly inexistent.  But because of its stable and high yield ''Chenopodium giganteum'' could be a plant of the future.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bhargava|first1=Atul|last2=Shukla|first2=Sudhir|last3=Ohri|first3=Deepak|date=2006-09-27|title=Evaluation of foliage yield and leaf quality traits in Chenopodium spp. in multiyear trials|journal=Euphytica|language=en|volume=153|issue=1–2|pages=199–213|doi=10.1007/s10681-006-9255-8|s2cid=38249440|issn=0014-2336}}</ref>

==Use==
The young shoots and leaves of ''Chenopodium giganteum'' can be eaten cooked like spinach, another member of the [[Amaranthaceae]]. Most of the [[oxalic acid]] and [[saponin]]s are removed during the cooking process, especially if boiled for 2 minutes at 100 °C (212 °F).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=ISHII|first1=YUUKO|last2=TAKIYAMA|first2=KAZUYOSHI|date=1991|title=CHARACTERIZATION OF OXALIC ACID IN VEGETABLES|journal=Analytical Sciences|language=en|volume=7|issue=Supple|pages=811–814|doi=10.2116/analsci.7.supple_811|issn=0910-6340|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Zheng|last2=Ando|first2=Akira|last3=Takeuchi|first3=Atsuko|last4=Ueda|first4=Hiroshi|date=2018|title=Effects of Cooking Conditions on the Relationships Among Oxalate, Nitrate, and Lutein in Spinach|journal=Food Science and Technology Research|language=en|volume=24|issue=3|pages=421–425|doi=10.3136/fstr.24.421|issn=1344-6606|doi-access=free}}</ref> However, the leaves are also edible raw in lower quantities, for example as a salad.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2011/jul/08/alys-fowler-tree-spinach|title=Alys Fowler: Tree spinach|last=Fowler|first=Alys|date=2011-07-08|website=the Guardian|language=en|access-date=2018-11-09}}</ref> The seeds can be prepared similar to [[rice]] or [[quinoa]] or can alternatively be ground into flour, which is then mixed with cereal flour for bread making.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://mansfeld.ipk-gatersleben.de/apex/f?p=185:46:0::NO::module,mf_use,source,akzanz,rehm,akzname,taxid:mf,,botnam,0,,Chenopodium+amaranticolor,421|title=Mansfeld World Database on Agricultural and Horticultural Crops|last=Gatersleben|first=Dr. Jörg Ochsmann, Dr. Gisela Weber, Dr. Ram Narang IPK|date=|website=mansfeld.ipk-gatersleben.de|language=de|access-date=2018-11-09}}</ref>

Due to the partially pink coloured leaves, ''Chenopodium giganteum'' also has an ornamental value.<ref name=":1" />

==Nutrition==
As common for species of the family [[Amaranthaceae]], the plants contain some amounts of [[saponin]]s and [[oxalic acid]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Chenopodium+giganteum|title=Chenopodium giganteum Tree Spinach PFAF Plant Database|website=pfaf.org|access-date=2018-11-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Al-Saleh|first1=G F S|last2=Gamal El-Din|first2=A Y|last3=Abbas|first3=J A|last4=Saeed|first4=N A|date=January 1997|title=Phytochemical and Biological Studies of Medicinal Plants in Bahrain: The Family Chenopodiaceae—Part 2|journal=International Journal of Pharmacognosy|language=en|volume=35|issue=1|pages=38–42|doi=10.1076/phbi.35.1.38.13266|issn=0925-1618|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Mroczek|first=Agnieszka|date=2015-01-24|title=Phytochemistry and bioactivity of triterpene saponins from Amaranthaceae family|journal=Phytochemistry Reviews|language=en|volume=14|issue=4|pages=577–605|doi=10.1007/s11101-015-9394-4|s2cid=7900797|issn=1568-7767}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Siener|first1=Roswitha|last2=Hönow|first2=Ruth|last3=Seidler|first3=Ana|last4=Voss|first4=Susanne|last5=Hesse|first5=Albrecht|date=January 2006|title=Oxalate contents of species of the Polygonaceae, Amaranthaceae and Chenopodiaceae families|journal=Food Chemistry|volume=98|issue=2|pages=220–224|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2005.05.059|issn=0308-8146}}</ref> which in high concentrations can have negative health impacts on humans (e.g. [[Hemolysis]] or [[Kidney stone disease]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://gestis.itrust.de/nxt/gateway.dll/gestis_de/017910.xml?f=templates$fn=default.htm$3.0|title=GESTIS Database|last=|first=|date=|website=gestis.itrust.de|language=en|access-date=2018-11-09}}</ref>
